newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Japan says may cut development aid to Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Japan says may cut development aid to Bangladesh.

text.p: Japan is likely to reduce development credit to Bangladesh, but may contribute up to $100 million to a proposed private sector infrastructure fund, a Japanese official said on Wednesday.

"The new Japanese government has reviewed ODA (overseas development assistance) and decided to reduce project loans," Takeo Matsuzawa, chief representative of the Overseas Economic Cooperation Fund of Japan, said in Dhaka.
Bangladesh had last month requested $700 million to finance development projects, but the Japanese government was unlikely to commit itself to providing it, he told reporters.
Matsuzawa said that development credit extended by Japan to Bangladesh so far totalled $4.556 billion. Of this, $600 million still remained unutilised, he said.
Bangladesh receives around $2.0 billion in international aid every year to finance its development projects and imports.
In reply to a question, Matsuzawa admitted that "any suspension of project credit to Bangladesh will affect its economy".
But he said that delays in the implementation of projects in Bangladesh meant that project costs kept rising.
Matsuzawa blamed Bangladesh's poor infrastructure for deterring foreign investment, citing in particular the frequency of power failures.
"If the infrastructure is not well prepared, investors will not come," he said, adding that Japan might contribute up to $100 million to the proposed $300 million private sector infrastructure fund.
The World Bank is expected to offer $150 million to the fund, officials with the Bangladesh Board of Investment said.
Japan, which offers Banagladesh an average of $200 million a year, is financing 12 major public sector development projects. These include power plants, telecommunications, bridge and airport works.
Japan has also invested $247 million in 13 private sector industrial projects in Bangladesh.

Bangladeshi officials say the country needs to raise the investment rate to 25 percent of the gross domestic product from the present 15-16 percent to spur economic growth to seven percent from the current 5.0 percent.
